title: Elizabeth of the Trinity (1880–1906)
hookLine: a young Carmelite who found heaven, she said, inside her own soul

cards: Heaven on earth. People say it about a beach at sunset, a first apartment, a plate of really good pasta. A young Carmelite in the French city of Dijon used the same phrase in a letter, and meant something stranger.
She had found her heaven on earth, she wrote, because heaven is God, and God is in the soul. Not a place to reach someday. A presence already home.
Her name in Carmel was Elizabeth of the Trinity, and today she is our word.

teach.b: First, the promise she built on.

At the Last Supper in John's Gospel, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any one love me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and will make our abode with him."

Father and Son, and Christian teaching adds the Spirit with them: the Trinity, not visiting but moving in. Elizabeth took that verse literally. Her spiritual life was learning to live with the guests already inside.
Second, her prayer. She wrote a prayer to the Trinity that begins, in English versions, O my God, Trinity whom I adore.
In it she asks to forget herself entirely, to be settled in God as still and peaceful as if her soul were already in eternity, and to let nothing draw her out. It isn't a prayer of requests.
It's a prayer of staying put. Third, her new name. In Saint Paul's letter to the Ephesians she found a phrase about Christians being made "unto the praise of his glory."

She took it, in Latin, as a name for herself: Laudem Gloriae, praise of glory. She wanted her life to be one long act of praise, even in the illness that ended it young. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary afternoon.
For Elizabeth, God isn't far away, waiting for a long climb.

teach.h: GOD NEARER THAN THE NEXT THOUGHT.
teach.b: God is nearer than the next thought, and prayer is turning around to notice. The Church later declared her a saint. Her prayer is still prayed in Carmels and in kitchens.

how: Catholics who follow Elizabeth of the Trinity pray her prayer to the Trinity, often in quiet before the Blessed Sacrament or at home, and use John 14:23 as a doorway into silent prayer.

games.q: what does “elizabeth of the trinity” mean?
o: a French queen who founded Carmelite convents
a Dijon Carmelite who prayed to God dwelling within
a medieval abbess who wrote on God's three persons

games.q: Elizabeth of the Trinity — tap the pairs.
p: because God is in the soul
O my God, Trinity whom I adore

s: Elizabeth taught that God must be found far away
she wrote that heaven is God, and God is in the soul.
she took a Latin name from Saint Paul
Laudem Gloriae, praise of glory, from the letter to the Ephesians.
her prayer to the Trinity is mostly a list of requests
it asks mainly to forget herself and stay settled in God.

games.q: you're a young Carmelite reading Jesus's words: we will come to him, and make our abode with him. how do you pray with it?
o: treat it as a promise for the end of time only.
live as if the guests are already inside, and turn toward them.
keep it as a nice verse for feast days.
games.why: Elizabeth took it literally. her prayer was learning to live with the Trinity already at home in the soul.

practice: Instead of sending your attention up or out, let it sink down, behind the breastbone, beneath the busy thoughts, into the quiet home Elizabeth pictured, with guests already there.
Nothing needs to happen: just turn toward that inner room and stay, and when a thought pulls you out, come back in, gently.
If you pray, say the verse slowly, we will come to him, and make our abode with him; if you don't, rest in the stillest place you can find inside.

wordCard.voice: Elizabeth of the Trinity. A Carmelite of Dijon who prayed to the Trinity dwelling within, and called herself praise of glory. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: praise of glory, from Ephesians 1:12, the name Elizabeth took for herself.

carryVoice: Your line: the trinity within. Not a visitor passing through, but someone already home. Until tomorrow.
